headline: Hemp: 14 GOP senators urge Trump to let 11 December ban stand
dek: Sen. Ted Budd and 13 Republicans told Trump to reject any delay or 'framework' for intoxicating hemp, as the White House asks Congress to save CBD.
key_points: Fourteen Republican senators led by Ted Budd wrote to President Trump on 20 November asking him to let the federal hemp change take effect on 11 December 2026.
The letter rejects any federal 'framework' for intoxicating hemp and asks Trump to oppose a delay in any upcoming spending bill.
The White House has asked Congress to protect non-intoxicating full-spectrum CBD in the stopgap bill that must pass by the same 11 December deadline.
Sen. Tom Cotton, the Senate's No. 3 Republican, warned a further delay could threaten the whole funding bill, The Hill reported.
body: The fight over hemp has moved inside the Republican Party. Fourteen Republican senators, led by Ted Budd of North Carolina, have written to President Donald Trump asking him to let the federal change to the definition of hemp take effect on 11 December 2026 as the law now provides, and to oppose any further delay. The letter is dated 20 November and Budd's office released it on 23 November.

The timing matters. The White House has just asked Congress to use the year-end stopgap spending bill to keep non-intoxicating full-spectrum CBD products legal, as we reported on 24 November. The senators are urging the President not to let that request grow into a broader rescue for intoxicating hemp products, which they call a loophole.
## What the letter asks

The senators make three requests. First, hold to the 11 December date: they note that Trump signed a one-month extension in September and say his administration made clear at the time there would be no more. Second, reject what they call a last-minute federal 'framework' for intoxicating hemp, which they describe as a permanent licence for the industry. Third, oppose any extension 'in any upcoming legislative vehicle', which in practice means the stopgap bill.

The letter grounds the case in the law Congress passed last year. Section 781 of Public Law 119-37, part of the bill that reopened the federal government a year ago, rewrote the hemp definition that the 2018 Farm Bill created. The senators say the Senate passed that change by 76 votes to 24, and that hemp farming for fiber, grain and seed stays protected. Their target is hemp converted into intoxicating THC products sold in gas stations, vape shops and convenience stores.

Budd was joined by Pete Ricketts, Tom Cotton, Kevin Cramer, Marsha Blackburn, James Lankford, Joni Ernst, John Cornyn, Mike Rounds, Mitch McConnell, Rick Scott, Chuck Grassley, Jim Banks and Cynthia Lummis. Budd's office paired the release with figures it attributes to emergency-department data, including a 461% rise in pediatric cannabis poisoning cases from 2018 to 2023.
> The hemp industry's fate now rides on a spending bill that has nothing to do with hemp, and on which side of his own party the President chooses.
## The spending bill is the battleground

Government funding runs out on 11 December, the same day the hemp change takes effect. The Hill reported on 25 November that the White House has sent Congress a list of items it wants in a stopgap bill that would run to 31 March. On hemp, the administration wants language that protects non-intoxicating products such as full-spectrum CBD while limiting access for children, without wiping out the industry.

There is also a bipartisan bill from Sens. Amy Klobuchar and Tim Sheehy that would create a regulatory framework for intoxicating hemp, which we covered on 18 November. The 14 signers oppose that approach. Their resistance to the first delay nearly derailed the September funding bill before it passed, The Hill reported. Cotton, the No. 3 Senate Republican, has said that adding a further delay to a funding deal could 'threaten the entire bill'.

The calendar is short. Congress returns next week. Senate Democrats hold their leadership election on 1 December, and talks on their side of the funding deal have largely waited on that result, according to The Hill. That leaves roughly a week and a half of working days to settle hemp along with defense and war-funding disputes.
## What changes on 11 December

If nothing passes, the new federal definition applies. As we reported earlier this month, it caps total THC at 0.4 milligrams per container for finished hemp products, a limit that would take most hemp-derived THC drinks, gummies and vapes off the federal books. Synthetic cannabinoids made from hemp were already pulled out of the legal definition on 12 November.

The White House request is narrow by comparison. Full-spectrum CBD is made from whole-plant extract and keeps the trace THC that occurs naturally in hemp, which is why the new cap reaches it; the administration's list asks Congress to keep those products on shelves, without naming a THC number. The senators' letter does not mention CBD directly. Its line in the sand is a framework for intoxicating products.

States are not waiting. As we reported on 20 November, a federal judge in Chicago declined to pause Illinois's own law moving hemp THC sales into licensed dispensaries. Maine and Vermont have also issued notices to the hemp trade ahead of 11 December, as we reported on 19 November.
## What it means for operators

For hemp brands and retailers, the letter narrows the realistic outcomes. A narrow CBD fix in the stopgap bill now looks like the most the White House can push without a fight inside its own conference. A broad delay or federal framework would have to get past 14 senators who say they will resist it, including the Senate's No. 3 Republican.

For licensed cannabis operators, the result cuts the other way. A ban on intoxicating hemp would remove a low-priced competitor in states where hemp THC has been sold alongside, or instead of, regulated marijuana.
## What to watch

Watch the text of the stopgap bill when Congress returns, and whether it carries any hemp language at all. Watch the Senate Democratic leadership vote on 1 December, which shapes the timing of a deal. And watch 11 December, when both government funding and the current federal hemp definition reach their deadline at the same time. Any White House response to the letter would be the clearest signal of where the President stands.
